name: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm

clinicalPearls: Ventricular ectopy spanning PVCs, nonsustained VT (NSVT), and accelerated idioventricular rhythm (AIVR) is very common and is most often asymptomatic, detected incidentally on telemetry or prompted by palpitations.

A PVC is a single ventricular beat occurring earlier than the next expected supraventricular beat; PVCs from one focus share an identical QRS morphology (unifocal), while differing morphologies indicate multifocal origin and raise suspicion for structural or myopathic disease.
Two consecutive ventricular beats form a couplet; three or more consecutive beats above 100/min define VT, and VT terminating spontaneously within 30 seconds is termed nonsustained.

QRS morphology localizes the focus: a dominant S wave in V1 (left bundle branch block-like) points to the right ventricle or septum, whereas a dominant R wave in V1 (right bundle branch block-like) points to the left ventricle; the frontal-plane axis distinguishes superior (inferior-wall) versus cranial origin.

Most ventricular arrhythmias without structural disease have a left bundle branch block-like pattern, while a right bundle branch block configuration or multiple PVC morphologies more often signal structural heart disease.

Idiopathic ectopy commonly arises from the right or left ventricular outflow tracts near the valve annuli, and also from papillary muscles and fascicular tissue; benign idiopathic NSVT is usually monomorphic with rates under 200/min.
Bigeminy (every other beat a PVC) can cause pseudobradycardia because the premature beats may not generate a palpable pulse, so counted rate can read falsely low.
In the peri-infarct period, PVCs and NSVT are common early manifestations of ischemia and can herald ventricular fibrillation.
AIVR is defined as three or more ventricular beats at a rate slower than 100/min, usually due to enhanced automaticity; it is common during acute MI and may emerge during sinus bradycardia or sleep.

Frequent ectopy can itself depress ventricular function (PVC-induced cardiomyopathy), but this rarely occurs unless PVCs account for at least 10-20% of total beats over 24 hours, and only a minority of such patients develop reversible cardiomyopathy.
Smooth, sharp QRS deflections of a PVC suggest a focus in relatively normal myocardium, whereas broad notching and slurring suggest a diseased substrate.
Recently inflammation has been recognized as contributing to PVC genesis in inflammatory and inherited cardiomyopathies.
harrison.pathophysiology: PVCs arise via enhanced (abnormal) automaticity, triggered activity, or localized reentry. They are frequently sympathetically sensitive and can reflect heightened sympathetic tone, myocardial ischemia, hypoxia, electrolyte disturbances (notably hypokalemia), or underlying structural heart disease. The site of earliest ventricular activation dictates the activation sequence and therefore the QRS morphology, allowing the surface ECG to suggest the anatomic origin and the likelihood of structural disease. In the setting of ischemia or structural disease, PVCs and NSVT can be harbingers of sustained VT or VF. AIVR is typically driven by automaticity, though rare reentrant circuits in diseased myocardium can produce it. PVC-induced ventricular dysfunction is thought to act through a mechanism akin to chronic tachycardia or through ventricular dyssynchrony.
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic outflow-tract or fascicular ventricular arrhythmia (benign)
Papillary muscle ectopy associated with mitral valve prolapse and mitral annular disjunction
Sustained monomorphic VT (must be distinguished from NSVT by duration and hemodynamic impact)
Supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction (wide-complex differential)
Genetic arrhythmia syndromes: long QT, Brugada, short QT, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
nonInfectiousMimics: Electrolyte abnormality (especially hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia) provoking ectopy
Stimulant or adrenergic effect (caffeine, alcohol, sympathomimetics)
Myocardial ischemia presenting as new ventricular ectopy
Drug or toxic effect on conduction (e.g., sodium-channel-blocking agents producing slowed, wide QRS rhythms)
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG in sinus rhythm (benign idiopathic arrhythmia usually shows a completely normal ECG; any abnormality warrants further workup)
Ambulatory/telemetry monitoring to quantify PVC burden and capture NSVT
Transthoracic echocardiography to assess ventricular function, wall-motion abnormalities, and valvular disease
Contrast-enhanced cardiac MRI to detect scar and late gadolinium enhancement suggesting underlying cardiomyopathy
Exercise stress testing for effort-related symptoms or coronary risk
Assessment of electrolytes (potassium, magnesium) during acute illness
Family history evaluation and consideration of genetic syndromes when a family history of sudden death exists
redFlags: Syncope or near-syncope, especially without prodrome, during exertion, or with an abnormal ECG or structural heart disease
Very rapid or polymorphic NSVT, or a 'short-coupled' first beat occurring before the peak of the T wave
Family history of sudden death prompting evaluation for inherited cardiomyopathy or channelopathy
Any abnormality on the 12-lead ECG (Q waves of prior infarction, ventricular hypertrophy, repolarization abnormalities of long QT/Brugada/ARVC)
Right bundle branch block-like or multifocal PVC morphology suggesting structural disease
Depressed ventricular function with frequent/repetitive ectopy
harrison.prognosis: PVCs, NSVT, and AIVR are most often benign when they occur in structurally normal hearts with normal ECGs, and idiopathic ectopy generally has excellent long-term arrhythmia-free outcomes (catheter ablation suppresses idiopathic PVCs in roughly 90% of patients). In contrast, the same arrhythmias carry prognostic weight in the presence of structural disease: after MI and in heart failure, frequent (typically >10 PVCs/h), repetitive PVCs, couplets, and NSVT are markers of depressed ventricular function and increased mortality, and they are likewise associated with worse outcomes in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and congenital heart disease with ventricular dysfunction. AIVR is usually well tolerated, though loss of AV synchrony may cause hemodynamic compromise in susceptible patients.
pitfalls: Bigeminal PVCs can produce pseudobradycardia, leading to an erroneously low measured heart rate.

Asymptomatic PVCs and NSVT discovered in a hospitalized or acutely ill patient generally do not require specific antiarrhythmic treatment beyond addressing the underlying illness and correcting aggravating factors.
Assuming all ventricular ectopy is benign; very rapid, polymorphic, short-coupled, or multifocal patterns and any ECG/structural abnormality demand evaluation for sudden-death risk.
Overlooking reversible PVC-induced cardiomyopathy in patients with very frequent ectopy and otherwise unexplained left ventricular dysfunction.
Attributing a wide-complex rhythm to VT without distinguishing it from supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy.
harrison.severityClassification: Risk is stratified less by ectopy count alone than by context: (1) structurally normal heart with normal ECG and monomorphic NSVT under 200/min - benign/low risk; (2) structural heart disease (post-MI, heart failure, HCM, congenital disease) where greater frequency and complexity (couplets, NSVT) mark more severe disease and higher mortality; (3) high-risk features warranting concern - syncope, very rapid/polymorphic/short-coupled NSVT, multifocal or RBBB-like morphology, abnormal ECG, or family history of sudden death. PVC burden of at least 10-20% of total beats over 24 hours is the threshold associated with potential PVC-induced ventricular dysfunction.
management: Reassurance without antiarrhythmic treatment for asymptomatic ectopy in a structurally normal heart with a normal ECG
Correct reversible provocateurs such as hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, ischaemia, hypoxia and stimulants including caffeine
For troublesome symptoms or a high ectopy burden, first-line beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers, with class I or class III antiarrhythmics as alternatives
Catheter ablation of the ectopic focus for a high PVC burden, PVC-induced cardiomyopathy or symptoms refractory to drug therapy
Evaluate for and treat underlying structural or ischaemic heart disease, considering an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator where sudden-death risk is high
Monitor PVC burden with ambulatory recording and left ventricular function with serial echocardiography
